The 10 MW blade from the AVATAR project was used in the present investigation.
The calculations were performed at a wind speed of 10.5 m/s and a rotational speed of 9.0218 rpm.
Grid convergence index (GCI) studies showed that the medium mesh with 10.9 million cells provided grid-converged results.
The FLOWer CFD results for power and thrust showed good agreement with numerical results from other project partners.
The 3D lift coefficients showed a significant increase (up to 40% radius) compared to the 2D airfoil data, demonstrating the rotational augmentation effect.
The rotational augmentation of the lift coefficient became smaller towards the blade tip due to the influence of trailing vortices.
The centrifugal force transports the separated flow at the near-hub region towards the middle part of the blade, reducing the wake size.
The Coriolis force delays the separation point, further contributing to the increase in lift coefficient.
Boundary layer codes like XFOIL have limitations in accurately predicting the aerodynamics of thick airfoils due to higher adverse pressure gradients.
The 3D CFD simulations showed a significant delay in the separation point and a reduction in the wake size at the inboard blade sections compared to the 2D case.
The rotational effects are influenced by the local solidity (chord-to-radius ratio) and the airfoil characteristics, in addition to the centrifugal and Coriolis forces.
The present work provides more information on the rotational augmentation occurring in the near-hub region of wind turbine blades.
The unsteady RANS simulations were performed using the SST-kω turbulence model, which provides reasonable accuracy for high adverse pressure gradient flows.
The calculations were conducted at a pitch angle of 0.0° to isolate the rotational effects from unsteady phenomena like dynamic stall.
The blade mesh was constructed using an automatic grid generator script, and the Chimera interpolation method was employed in the overlapping grid areas.
